practicality.justification: Provides an implementable visitor-level A/B test, named tooling, clear control and treatment, merchandising suggestions, and a profit-focused evaluation over 30 days. It appropriately allows an inconclusive result when traffic is insufficient. However, it lacks a concrete setup/review schedule and a low-traffic fallback suitable for a small operator.
quotes: Run an A/B split by visitor, 50/50
Variant: free shipping on orders of $95 or more.
If 30 days won't get you there, extend the test. Don't call it early.
practicality.improvement: Specify prelaunch checks, weekly data-quality reviews, and a day-30 decision process, including retaining the control offer if results remain inconclusive.

specificity.justification: Uses the supplied economics correctly to calculate discount erosion and a $93.40 profit-neutral threshold for a representative $72 order, then recommends an exact $95 offer. It identifies appropriate primary and secondary metrics. The decision rule is less precise than the offer: 'roughly 90%' confidence and 'not meaningfully higher' returns lack an explicit statistical method or numerical guardrail. The profit formula also leaves shipping receipts and net-versus-gross revenue treatment ambiguous.
quotes: A 15% discount takes $10.80 per order out of margin, leaving about $19.44.
That puts the profit-neutral threshold at about $93.40.
(Revenue − COGS − shipping you absorb − payment fees − discounts − refunds/returns) ÷ unique visitors
Adopt the threshold if the variant's contribution per visitor beats control with reasonable confidence, roughly 90% or better.
specificity.improvement: Define contribution using net merchandise revenue plus shipping collected minus actual shipping and other variable costs, avoiding double-counted discounts or refunds. Prespecify a confidence interval for profit-per-visitor lift and a numerical returns guardrail.

risk_awareness.justification: Addresses subsidy leakage to existing high-value orders, increased shipping costs, cart-padding returns, inadequate sample size, competing promotions, and weekday effects, with useful controls. However, the claim that every bumped-up order is profitable overgeneralizes average-margin arithmetic, and recovered carts are not necessarily 'pure upside' after all variable costs. The conversion-based sample-size estimate does not establish adequate power for the actual profit-per-visitor endpoint.
quotes: you'll be giving $9 to customers who didn't need the incentive
Bigger orders may cost more than $9 to ship, so use actual label costs.
Watch for people padding carts to qualify and then returning items.
Don't run other promotions during the test.
every recovered abandoned cart is pure upside.
risk_awareness.improvement: Qualify the threshold math by item-level margin and incremental basket size, estimate power using profit-per-visitor variance, maintain persistent visitor assignments, and account for delayed returns before declaring a winner.

overall_impression: Strong, actionable recommendation with sound first-pass economics and a useful profit-centered experiment. More precise accounting, statistical decision rules, and small-store execution details would make it exceptional.
